courseEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courseEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courseEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops academic writing, source appraisal and the use of evidence in arguments.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Economics
courseEvidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
courseEvidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling
courseEvidence.contribution: supplies concrete economic mechanisms for evaluating claims about markets and the state

courseEvidence.name: Logic & Discrete Mathematics
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on mathematics of decision‑making, covering topics in discrete mathematics such as logic, patterns and structures, with applications to computer science and algorithm construction.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces formal logic, abstract mathematical reasoning and proof. Students analyze propositions and quantified statements, work with sets, Boolean algebra, functions and relations, and develop direct and indirect proofs. Induction and recursive definitions extend these tools to mathematical structures. The final component systematically models processes and games without chance and investigates the existence and construction of winning strategies.
courseEvidence.topics: Propositional and predicate logic; Truth tables and logical laws; Set theory; Boolean algebra and circuits; Quantifiers; Functions and relations; Proof strategies; Mathematical induction; Recursive definitions; Games without chance and winning strategies; Process modelling
courseEvidence.methods: Truth-table analysis; Direct proof and proof by cases; Proof by contrapositive and contradiction; Proof with quantifiers; Mathematical induction; Formal process and game modelling
courseEvidence.contribution: Studies propositions, quantified statements, Boolean algebra and proof. It applies these tools to discrete mathematics and computational reasoning.

courseEvidence.name: Governance of Sustainability
courseEvidence.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
courseEvidence.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
courseEvidence.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
courseEvidence.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives
courseEvidence.contribution: analyses governance choices in sustainability transitions

courseEvidence.name: Climate Change
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
courseEvidence.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
courseEvidence.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model
courseEvidence.contribution: grounds climate responsibility in scientific accounts of climate change

courseEvidence.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
courseEvidence.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
courseEvidence.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
courseEvidence.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment
courseEvidence.contribution: Uses life-cycle assessment to compare environmental, social, health and cost impacts of products and processes. These findings inform questions of responsibility and policy.

courseEvidence.name: Modern History
courseEvidence.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
courseEvidence.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
courseEvidence.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
courseEvidence.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development
courseEvidence.contribution: situates modern political and philosophical ideas in historical change

courseEvidence.name: Native American Histories
courseEvidence.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
courseEvidence.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
courseEvidence.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production
courseEvidence.contribution: examines Indigenous-centered histories and colonial knowledge, a concrete intercultural context

courseEvidence.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
courseEvidence.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
courseEvidence.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: examines the philosophical foundations and interpretation of human rights

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
courseEvidence.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life
courseEvidence.methods: Close reading of philosophical texts; Conceptual analysis; Philosophical argument reconstruction and evaluation; Argumentative essay development
courseEvidence.contribution: surveys philosophical questions and traditions as the broad disciplinary entry point

courseEvidence.name: Ethics
courseEvidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
courseEvidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
courseEvidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development
courseEvidence.contribution: examines duties, rights and ethical reasoning through cases such as climate change

courseEvidence.name: Philosophy of Mind
courseEvidence.description2: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.
courseEvidence.topics: Persons and personal identity; Psychological and narrative theories of identity; Buddhist non-self; Split-brain cases and self-knowledge; Behaviourism; Physicalism and functionalism; Mind-body problem; Content externalism and internalism; AI intelligence and consciousness; Virtual reality; Dreaming and perception; Transformative experience; Value of conscious experience; Animal minds
courseEvidence.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual analysis; Reconstruction and evaluation of arguments; Comparison of theories of mind; Literature-based philosophical research
courseEvidence.contribution: studies consciousness, personal identity and the mind-body problem

courseEvidence.name: Philosophy of Emotion
courseEvidence.description2: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
courseEvidence.topics: Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories of emotion; Ancient Greek and Indian accounts of emotion; Epistemic emotions; Emotion and decision-making; Love; Fear and existential anxiety; Mood and grief; Moral emotions; Gender and emotion; Political love and anger; Racial injustice; Temporality of emotion; Emotion and artistic expression
courseEvidence.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual and argumentative analysis; Phenomenological description of emotional experience; Critical comparison of emotion theories
courseEvidence.contribution: Investigates the nature, rationality and ethical, political and aesthetic significance of emotions; a substantive philosophical extension beyond mind, not a duplicate introductory mind course.

courseEvidence.name: Free Will, Time & the Self
courseEvidence.description2: Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.
courseEvidence.profile: Explores free will and agency in relation to time and the self. Historical Greek and Indian perspectives introduce debates about fatalism, determinism, compatibility and moral responsibility; later topics include scientific challenges, addiction, luck and agency in games. The second part examines the reality and experience of time, physics and temporal asymmetries, then developing research linking time, action and selfhood. Essays require close source analysis and an independent argument.
courseEvidence.topics: Free will and fatalism; Foreknowledge and determinism; Compatibilism and rival theories; Moral responsibility; Greek and Indian accounts of agency; Scientific perspectives on free will; Addiction and the self; Moral luck; Games and agency; Value capture; Reality and experience of time; Time and physics; Temporal asymmetries and bias; Time, action and selfhood
courseEvidence.methods: Conceptual analysis; Close philosophical reading; Argument reconstruction and evaluation; Literature-based philosophical research
courseEvidence.contribution: investigates free will, time, agency and the self

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
courseEvidence.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
courseEvidence.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice
courseEvidence.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction
courseEvidence.contribution: reads political-philosophy texts and develops normative arguments about political life

courseEvidence.name: Theory of International Relations
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
courseEvidence.topics: International state system and non-state actors; Classical and contemporary geopolitics; Realism and neorealism; Liberalism and neoliberalism; Marxism and world-systems theory; Constructivism and critical theory; Foreign-policy decision-making; War and great-power competition; Colonialism and economic relations; Climate politics; UN Security Council diplomacy
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-guided international case analysis; Historical-source analysis; Comparative foreign-policy analysis; Country-position and strategy research; Diplomatic negotiation simulation; Position-paper and resolution drafting
courseEvidence.contribution: International-relations theories and a UN simulation supply empirical political applications, not an additional philosophical theory sequence.

courseEvidence.name: European Union Politics
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces EU politics. Outlines actors, institutions and decision‑making rules; examines responses to crises; and employs various approaches to study EU politics and policy‑making.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
courseEvidence.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience
courseEvidence.methods: EU policy and legislative-document research; Process tracing; Systematic amendment coding; Ideology and amendment-activity analysis; Salience assessment; Comparative news-source analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: EU institutions, interest groups and a legislative-dossier research project provide governance context, not specialist philosophical analysis.

courseEvidence.name: Peace & Conflict
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
courseEvidence.topics: Conflict theories and structural violence; Identity and historical grievances; Colonialism and forced migration; International peace and security; Humanitarian law and human rights; Positive, negative and hybrid peace; Local peacebuilding; Frozen conflicts; Counterterrorism and rule of law; Transitional justice; Gender and conflict; Development and peacebuilding; Reconciliation, arts and religion; Global South perspectives; Travelling concepts and researcher positionality
courseEvidence.methods: Interdisciplinary Research Process; Cross-disciplinary travelling-concept analysis; Conflict case analysis; Context and stakeholder mapping; Annotated bibliography and evidence synthesis; Policy-option appraisal; Policy-brief and background-dossier development; Researcher positionality analysis; Comparative research podcast production
courseEvidence.contribution: Conflict theories, peacebuilding and travelling concepts provide social-scientific applications of justice and reconciliation, not dedicated normative philosophy.

courseEvidence.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courseEvidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
courseEvidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: Teaches empirical qualitative research design, data collection/analysis, interpretation and reflexivity. It is a complementary research method, not philosophical epistemology, argument analysis or a philosophy thesis.

courseEvidence.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
courseEvidence.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
courseEvidence.contribution: examines environmental justice and collective action as ethical-political problems

courseEvidence.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courseEvidence.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
courseEvidence.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
courseEvidence.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
courseEvidence.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design
courseEvidence.contribution: trains analysis and construction of persuasive arguments

courseEvidence.name: Style & Meaning
courseEvidence.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
courseEvidence.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
courseEvidence.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence
courseEvidence.contribution: Linguistic stylistics studies choices that shape literary and nonfiction meaning; interpretive complement, not analytic philosophy or philosophical argument validation.

courseEvidence.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
courseEvidence.description2: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
courseEvidence.contribution: studies communication and representation of the climate crisis

courseEvidence.name: Rhetoric in Action
courseEvidence.description2: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
courseEvidence.profile: Applies rhetoric through community-engaged work with local primary-school children. Students develop their own public-speaking, debating and storytelling skills, then design and iteratively refine age-appropriate teaching activities with school partners. On-site coaching and a final public-speaking event connect rhetorical education to civic participation and confidence. Structured reflection examines reciprocity, cultural sensitivity, personal development and the practical challenges of community-engaged teaching.
courseEvidence.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning
courseEvidence.methods: Public-speaking and debate coaching; Storytelling exercises; Iterative design and revision of teaching materials; Practice-based rhetorical instruction; Gibbs reflective-cycle analysis; Public-speaking event design and evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: Applies rhetorical teaching with local primary-school children. Interaction is principally Dutch; this community exercise is not a philosophy teaching qualification.

courseEvidence.name: Persuasive Communication
courseEvidence.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
courseEvidence.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
courseEvidence.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle
courseEvidence.contribution: Examines framing, nudging and cognitive shortcuts together with ethical theories of persuasion and community communication work. No named future partner or project is guaranteed.

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
courseEvidence.description2: Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
courseEvidence.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
courseEvidence.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development
courseEvidence.contribution: Ancient material production, technologies and identities supply historical context only, not ancient Greek/Sanskrit/Chinese philosophy.

courseEvidence.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
courseEvidence.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
courseEvidence.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
courseEvidence.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design
courseEvidence.contribution: analyzes ancient democracy and contested heritage in political and historical context

courseEvidence.name: Great Literary Works
courseEvidence.description2: Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.
courseEvidence.profile: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.
courseEvidence.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
courseEvidence.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration
courseEvidence.contribution: practises close reading of influential literary texts across periods as interpretive complement

courseEvidence.name: World Myth & Literature
courseEvidence.description2: Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
courseEvidence.profile: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
courseEvidence.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation
courseEvidence.contribution: Compares global literary myths and narrative transmission. It does not replace world philosophies or comparative theology.

courseEvidence.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
courseEvidence.description2: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
courseEvidence.contribution: examines theories of meaning and interpretation through close readings, a complement to philosophical text seminars

courseEvidence.name: Media & the Environment
courseEvidence.description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.
courseEvidence.topics: Environmental representation; Anthropocene; Animal representation and human-nonhuman relations; Deep time and ecological temporality; Biocentrism and environmental justice; Contested ideas of nature; Indigenous and postcolonial media; Ecological risk and scientific knowledge; Environmental affect and perception; Agency, scale and responsibility; Sustainability discourse
courseEvidence.methods: Close film, image and sound analysis; Comparative analysis of media forms and representational strategies; Ecocritical interpretation; Theory-based analytical or creative media inquiry
courseEvidence.contribution: examines mediated representations of nature and environmental politics

comparability: Both options develop philosophy through introductory historical argument, normative ethics, philosophy of mind, agency and political philosophy. Advanced essays on free will and emotion are specifically philosophical. Legal philosophy, logic and rhetorical analysis add compatible methods. Historical, media and empirical courses are complementary. The climate option gives applied evidence for normative questions through climate science, justice, media, markets, life-cycle impact and governance. No broader option sustains a third distinct philosophy concentration. VU retains deeper historical, intercultural, science, epistemology, text-seminar and thesis coverage.
repair: Move Rhetoric in Action to term six and Peace & Conflict to term four. Move introductory economics into term one and Political Philosophy to term three in the climate option. Use Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy in term three and move Human Rights: Law & Philosophy to term five to replace the unavailable delta project. Reassess alignment, logic and metaphysics claims.

stoppingDecision.assessment: Two defensible options use philosophy as the taught subject, including six dedicated philosophy courses in each, complemented by legal philosophy and logic. The second option offers a distinct application in climate ethics and public reasoning. A mind-and-knowledge direction would rely on the same philosophy courses and shift toward empirical psychology if extended. The Dutch religion and governance variants do not establish additional routes within the English comparator.
